Economy just means she can convey deep meaning with very few words, creating an entire universe in just a couple paragraphs. In Jacob's story, he is happy for seven years but then agonizes for the last seven because he doesn't want to be with Leah; he wants Rachel instead. This economy of language also includes irony, which makes it funny.

The Bible was conceived as a humorous story about two sisters who hate each other and compete for the same man. When Rachel sees that Jacob has no children by her, she envies Leah and tells Jacob to get her pregnant. So, she gives him her maid, who conceives and bears Jacob a son. Then, Rachel says God has judged her, giving her a son through the maid.

This is a comedy where Rachel tries to outcompete Leah with her own child. When Jacob gets his second son from the maid, Rachel claims it as hers. She continues to compete with Leah by cheering for her son's success. This is all meant to be a beautiful story that provokes deep reflection and creativity.

The Jews are known for their creativity and dominance in media, academia, and Hollywood because they grow up with these profound stories that force them to think deeply about life. The story of David starts when Samuel, a prophet, finds him in Jesse's house and proclaims he will be Israel's king. David defeats Goliath early on but later becomes jealous of Saul, forcing him to run away. Eventually, Saul is killed, and David returns to become king.

This class reveals that the Bible's account of David as a favored king is propaganda; the real story is that Saul is king, David is a popular mercenary who kills Saul and then takes the throne. The Yahwist or J, a court historian, wrote Genesis to legitimize David’s kingship by painting him in a more favorable light.
